small_guidance:
- The current kernel reloads the same x values for every (oh, ow) in the spatial tile because each program only computes BLOCK_N output points scattered across the batch/H/W. Switch to a 2D output-spatial tile (BLOCK_OH × BLOCK_OW per program, plus a batch axis) so KH×KW input loads are shared across the tile via shifted base pointers — should cut global load traffic ~9×.
- Add larger/wider configs targeting the (B*OH*OW=128*126*126≈2M, OC=64, IC*KH*KW=72) shape: try BLOCK_OC=64 fixed (matches OC exactly, eliminates oc-mask), with BLOCK_N up to 256/512 and num_warps=8, num_stages=3-4. Drop configs with BLOCK_OC>64 since OC=64.
- Move output store address math to use the original x_base linear index rather than recomputing b/oh/ow products; and ensure x is stored channels-last or pre-transpose so input loads along ic become contiguous (currently each ic step jumps H*W=16384 elements, defeating coalescing within a row tile).
large_guidance:
- Redesign as an implicit-GEMM with one program per (batch, OC-tile, OH×OW-tile-in-2D). Tile output as (BLOCK_OH, BLOCK_OW) e.g. 8×16 or 4×32; load a single (BLOCK_OH+KH-1)×(BLOCK_OW+KW-1) input patch per ic into registers/SMEM and reuse it across the KH·KW taps and the OC tile. This exploits the heavy spatial reuse the current pointwise-N tiling misses.
- Fold the bias add, divide-by-constant, and leaky_relu into the epilogue (already done) but also fuse the divisor into the weight at init (`weight_scaled = weight / divisor`, `bias_scaled = bias / divisor`) to remove a per-element multiply — this is a legal constant-folding of a scalar, not an algebraic shortcut on a heavy op.
- Use channels-last (NHWC) input/output layout so the IC reduction loop reads contiguous vectors of length IC=8 per spatial position; with IC=8 you can fully unroll the IC loop and issue one vec8 load per (kh,kw), turning the inner K=72 reduction into 9 tl.dot-friendly chunks. Consider tl.dot on a reshaped (BLOCK_TILE, IC*KH*KW) × (IC*KH*KW, BLOCK_OC) matmul with im2col computed via pointer arithmetic.
